analysis.one_liner: Requires all health care providers to publicly post the cash prices of their services.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee in February 2020 and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required every business that sells health care items, services, or procedures to the public — hospitals, doctors, drug makers, device sellers — to continuously disclose the actual cash prices for what they sell, posted openly at the point of purchase, in print, and online [S2] [S3]. The goal was to let patients see what care costs before buying it, something the health care industry generally does not show. The bill went nowhere: it was read twice, sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and sat there until the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and consumers shopping for health care. Anyone paying out of pocket — the uninsured, people with high-deductible plans, people paying cash — would be able to see prices before receiving care, instead of getting a bill weeks later. Employers and insurers negotiating with hospitals would also gain a benchmark for what things really cost.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying out of pocket for care

how_it_helps.text: Requires all public providers of health care items, products, services, and procedures to disclose their cash prices on a continuous basis, in an open and conspicuous manner [S3].
Prices must be available at the point of purchase, in print, and on the internet, so patients could comparison-shop before receiving care rather than after [S2] [S3].
The scope is broad: it covers the whole health care industry, not just hospitals, so drug prices, device prices, and procedure prices would all be public [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, physician practices, drug manufacturers, and device and supply sellers, which would have to compile and continuously publish prices and would lose the ability to charge patients different unpublicized amounts. Patients indirectly, if providers responded by nudging listed cash prices upward toward their highest negotiated rates.

drawbacks.text: Posting cash prices does not reveal the negotiated rates insurers actually pay, so for most insured patients the disclosed price could still differ sharply from what their plan pays — transparency alone may not lower what most people owe.
Compliance would impose real administrative costs on providers, who would have to maintain and continuously update public price lists for every item, service, and procedure they offer [S3].

If disclosed cash prices become a reference point, some providers might respond by raising their lowest cash prices toward their highest negotiated rates, narrowing savings for the uninsured rather than cutting prices overall.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients who pay cash or have high-deductible coverage, the bill offered a direct, practical benefit: knowing the price before receiving care. Its weakness is that it only covers cash prices, not the negotiated rates that drive most insured people's costs, so it is a transparency floor rather than a full fix. The compliance burden on providers is real but modest compared with what patients stand to gain from price visibility. The larger problem with the bill is that it never got a hearing or a vote, so none of these tradeoffs were ever tested on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee in February 2020, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Cassidy introduced the Transparent Health Care Pricing Act of 2020 on February 13, 2020 [S1] [S5].

The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where it stayed for the remainder of the 116th Congress with no hearing, markup, or floor vote [S5].
The bill would have required health care providers to disclose cash prices for items, products, services, and procedures at the point of purchase, in print, and online [S2] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, drug makers, and other health care providers came out ahead, because they kept selling care without having to show patients the price first.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and providers, whose prices stayed hidden

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require public disclosure of health care cash prices and referred it to his party's path in the Senate.

for.name: 2 of 53 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Senate support it attracted.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for health legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 13, 2020 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill, so no partisan split is recorded; its sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans.

industries.note: They would have had to publish cash prices for everything they sell, ending the practice of presenting patients with costs only after care is delivered. Their interest ran against the patients who would gain price visibility.
The bill covered providers of health care products to the public, so drug prices would have had to be posted openly, making it harder to charge different patients sharply different amounts.
Device and supply prices would have had to be publicly disclosed, exposing markups that patients currently cannot see before purchase.
